q: A non-financial enterprise had earlier granted long-term loans to other parties. During the year, those parties repay the loans in cash. In the enterprise's cash flow statement under AS-3, the amount repaid is a cash flow from:

options.C: Financing activities
options.D: No activity, since loans are not part of its business

e: For a non-financial enterprise, granting and recovering long-term loans is an investing activity, so cash repaid by the borrowers is an investing inflow under AS-3.

q: A non-financial enterprise purchases shares which it holds purely for dealing and trading purposes, expecting to resell them shortly at a profit. Under AS-3, the purchase of such securities is classified as a cash flow from:

options.C: Operating activities, the securities being held for trading
options.D: No activity, since the shares may be resold within the same year

e: Securities held purely for dealing or trading are like stock-in-trade of the enterprise, so their purchase is an operating activity cash flow under AS-3.

q: A lessee enterprise makes a payment under a finance lease, of which a part represents the principal (capital) element of the lease obligation. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, the principal element is classified as a cash flow from:

options.C: Investing activities
options.D: No activity, since no asset has been purchased for cash

e: The principal element of a finance lease payment repays a financing obligation, so it is a financing activity outflow under AS-3 (only the interest element may differ).

q: An enterprise raises a short-term bank loan, repayable after nine months, which does not form part of its day-to-day cash management arrangements. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, the proceeds of the loan are classified as a cash flow from:

options.C: No activity, since the loan is short-term in nature
options.D: Financing activities

e: A bank loan that is not part of day-to-day cash management (not a cash equivalent) is a borrowing, so its proceeds are a financing activity inflow under AS-3.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 3,00,000. During the year, its accrued income decreased by Rs 20,000, its prepaid expenses increased by Rs 15,000 and its bills payable decreased by Rs 25,000. Its cash generated from operations (before tax) is:
e: Cash generated = Rs 3,00,000 + Rs 20,000 (accrued income decrease, cash received) - Rs 15,000 (prepaid increase) - Rs 25,000 (bills payable decrease, cash paid) = Rs 2,80,000.

q: In preparing a fund flow statement, the increase during a year in the balance of the accumulated depreciation (provision for depreciation) account is sometimes mistakenly treated as a source of funds. The correct position is that it is:

options.A: A source of funds, because depreciation is a charge against profits
options.B: An application of funds, because the assets of the enterprise are being consumed
options.C: Shown as a separate source only when the enterprise has earned a net profit
options.D: Not a source of funds by itself; the depreciation charged for the year is merely added back to profits in computing the funds from operations

e: An increase in accumulated depreciation is not itself a source of funds; the depreciation charged is merely added back to profit in computing funds from operations.

q: A non-financial enterprise sells the patent rights held by it and receives cash for them. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, the amount received is classified as a cash flow from:

options.C: Financing activities
options.D: Extraordinary activities, shown outside the three-fold classification

e: Patent rights are a long-term asset, so cash received on selling them is an investing activity inflow under AS-3.

q: An enterprise purchases goods on credit during a year but makes no payment to the suppliers within that year. In its cash flow statement for that year, this purchase:

options.A: Appears as an outflow under operating activities at the full purchase value
options.B: Appears as an inflow under financing activities
options.C: Is adjusted only in the schedule of changes in working capital
options.D: Does not appear at all, since a cash flow statement records only actual movements of cash

e: A cash flow statement records only actual cash movements; a credit purchase with no payment involves no cash flow and does not appear at all.

q: An enterprise places a sum in a bank deposit having an original maturity of one year. For the purpose of its cash flow statement under AS-3, the amount so placed is:

options.A: Treated as a cash equivalent, so that no cash flow is reported
options.B: Treated as a cash equivalent if the deposit can be broken before maturity
options.C: Reported as an outflow under financing activities
options.D: Not a cash equivalent, and its placement is reported as an outflow under investing activities

e: A deposit with original maturity of one year exceeds the short maturity (about three months) allowed for cash equivalents, so it is not a cash equivalent and its placement is an investing outflow.

q: An enterprise reports a negative cash flow from operating activities year after year, although it continues in business by selling investments and raising fresh loans. The sound interpretation of this position is that:

options.A: Its accounting profits must necessarily have been negative in each year
options.B: Negative operating cash flow is normal for all growing enterprises and calls for no concern
options.C: Its core operations are not generating cash and its survival depends on non-operating sources, which is not sustainable in the long run
options.D: Its fund flow statement will necessarily also show a decrease in working capital every year

e: Persistent negative operating cash flow means core operations do not generate cash and survival depends on selling investments and raising loans, which cannot continue indefinitely.

q: Cost accounting is distinguished from management accounting mainly in that cost accounting:

options.A: Is concerned with providing information for planning, control and decision-making at all levels of management
options.B: Is primarily concerned with the ascertainment of the cost of products, services and processes
options.C: Is not based on any recorded cost data and relies wholly on estimates of the future
options.D: Covers the preparation and presentation of the financial statements of the enterprise

e: Cost accounting is primarily concerned with ascertaining the cost of products, services and processes, whereas management accounting serves wider planning, control and decision-making.

q: A worker is paid wages (basic pay and dearness allowance) of Rs 30,000 for a month. The employer's contributions and welfare expenditure in respect of the worker amount to 20 per cent of the wages. The worker works for 240 hours during the month. The total labour cost per hour of the worker is:

options.C: Rs 150
options.D: Rs 100

e: Total labour cost = Rs 30,000 + 20% of Rs 30,000 = Rs 36,000; per hour = Rs 36,000 / 240 hours = Rs 150.

q: A Goods Received Note, prepared when materials are received into the stores, serves mainly to:

options.A: Record the quantity of material received and accepted, and form the basis for entering the receipt in the stores records and checking the supplier's bill for payment
options.B: Authorise the storekeeper to issue material to a production department
options.C: Record the quantity of material returned by a production department as surplus
options.D: Fix the price at which materials are to be issued to production

e: The Goods Received Note records the quantity of material received and accepted, bases the stores record entry and supports checking the supplier bill before payment.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 10,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 200 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the total annual ordering and carrying cost when orders are placed in economic order quantities is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 10,000 x Rs 200 / Rs 4) = 1,000 units; ordering cost = 10 orders x Rs 200 = Rs 2,000 and carrying cost = 500 units average x Rs 4 = Rs 2,000, total Rs 4,000.

q: A purchase requisition in a factory is a document which:

options.A: Is sent by the purchase department to a supplier, ordering the supply of specified materials
options.B: Is prepared by the supplier, acknowledging the order placed by the factory
options.C: Records the materials actually received into the stores after inspection
options.D: Is raised by the storekeeper (or a consuming department) and sent to the purchase department, authorising it to procure the materials specified

e: A purchase requisition is raised by the storekeeper or consuming department and sent to the purchase department, authorising it to procure the specified materials.

q: The annual demand for a material is 8,000 units, the cost of placing an order is Rs 100 and the purchase price is Rs 50 per unit, the carrying cost being 20 per cent per annum of the purchase price. A supplier offers a discount of 4 per cent on the price if orders are placed in lots of 2,000 units or more. The total annual cost (purchase, ordering and carrying) if the discount offer is accepted is:
e: Discounted price = Rs 50 x 96% = Rs 48; purchase = 8,000 x Rs 48 = Rs 3,84,000, ordering = 4 orders x Rs 100 = Rs 400, carrying = 1,000 units average x Rs 9.60 = Rs 9,600; total = Rs 3,94,000.

q: When a production department finds that material drawn by it is in excess of its requirement and returns the surplus to the stores, the document used for the return, on the basis of which the job is credited and the stores record is updated, is the:

options.C: Material return note
options.D: Bin card

e: Surplus material returned by a department to stores is documented on a material return note, on which the job is credited and the stores record is updated.

q: After primary distribution, the overhead totals are: Production Department X — Rs 2,00,000; Production Department Y — Rs 1,60,000; Service Department S1 (Stores) — Rs 40,000; Service Department S2 (Canteen) — Rs 20,000. Under the step method, S2 is closed first on the basis of employees: 50 per cent to X, 30 per cent to Y and 20 per cent to S1. S1 is then closed on the basis of material issues: 60 per cent to X and 40 per cent to Y. The total overhead of Production Department X after secondary distribution is:
e: S2 Rs 20,000 goes Rs 10,000 to X, Rs 6,000 to Y and Rs 4,000 to S1; S1 then totals Rs 44,000, of which 60% (Rs 26,400) goes to X; X total = Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 10,000 + Rs 26,400 = Rs 2,36,400.

q: An impersonal cost centre, as distinct from a personal cost centre, is a cost centre which:

options.A: Consists of a person or a group of persons responsible for the costs incurred
options.B: Consists of a location or an item of equipment (or a group of these), rather than a person
options.C: Is located outside the factory premises
options.D: Incurs only indirect costs and no direct costs

e: An impersonal cost centre consists of a location or an item of equipment (or a group of these), whereas a personal cost centre consists of a person or group of persons.

q: A product sells at Rs 250 per unit. Its variable cost is Rs 140 per unit and, in addition, a sales commission of 10 per cent of the selling price is payable on every unit sold. Fixed costs are Rs 3,40,000. The break-even point in units is:

options.C: 2,430 units
options.D: 5,667 units

e: Contribution per unit = Rs 250 - Rs 140 - commission 10% of Rs 250 (Rs 25) = Rs 85; break-even = Rs 3,40,000 / Rs 85 = 4,000 units.

q: On the receipt of materials, a part of the consignment is found, on inspection, to be damaged and is rejected and returned to the supplier. To claim credit from the supplier for the value of the rejected material, the stores issues to the supplier a:

options.C: Credit note in favour of the supplier
options.D: Debit note, debiting the supplier's account with the value of the material rejected

e: Rejected material returned to the supplier is supported by a debit note debiting the supplier account with its value, so that credit can be claimed from the supplier.

q: A material is ordered in lots of 1,500 units. Its purchase price is Rs 30 per unit and the carrying cost is 10 per cent per annum of the value of the stock held. The annual carrying (holding) cost of the material is:
e: Average stock = 1,500 / 2 = 750 units, value = 750 x Rs 30 = Rs 22,500; annual carrying cost = 10% of Rs 22,500 = Rs 2,250.

q: Under the non-integral (interlocking) system, where separate cost and financial books are maintained, the profits shown by the two sets of books are reconciled through:

options.A: The General Ledger Adjustment Account in the cost ledger
options.B: A Memorandum Reconciliation Account, which does not form part of the double entry system of either set of books
options.C: The Stores Ledger Control Account in the financial books
options.D: The Cost Ledger Control Account in the cost ledger

e: Under the non-integral system the two profit figures are reconciled through a Memorandum Reconciliation Account, which is outside the double entry system of both sets of books.

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a department are Rs 3,00,000 for 20,000 budgeted hours. The actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 3,20,000. During the period, 400 hours were lost as abnormal idle time. The fixed overhead idle time variance is:

options.C: Rs 20,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)

e: Standard fixed overhead rate = Rs 3,00,000 / 20,000 hours = Rs 15 per hour; idle time variance = 400 hours x Rs 15 = Rs 6,000 adverse.

q: Operation costing, as distinct from operating (service) costing, is a method which:

options.A: Is used by undertakings rendering services, such as transport and hospitals, and uses a composite cost unit
options.B: Ascertains the cost of a service per passenger-kilometre or per patient-day
options.C: Is a hybrid of job and process costing, under which costs are collected operation-wise for products that pass through a number of distinct operations
options.D: Is used only where a single homogeneous product is produced on a mass scale

e: Operation costing is a hybrid of job and process costing in which costs are collected operation-wise for products passing through a number of distinct operations.

q: A bus with 48 seats runs 250 kilometres a day for 25 days in a month. The average occupancy is 80 per cent of the seating capacity. The total operating cost for the month is Rs 4,80,000. The operating cost per passenger-kilometre is:
e: Passenger-kilometres = 48 seats x 250 km x 25 days x 80% = 2,40,000; cost per passenger-km = Rs 4,80,000 / 2,40,000 = Rs 2.00.

q: Material issued to a job is later returned to the stores as surplus. In the stores records, the returned material is taken back into stock and the job is credited at:

options.A: The current replacement price of the material on the date of return
options.B: The price at which the material was originally issued to the job
options.C: The average price of all the lots of the material held in stock
options.D: The lowest price at which any lot of the material was purchased

e: Returned material is taken back into stock and the job credited at the price at which it was originally issued to the job, reversing the original charge exactly.

q: A firm expects sales of Rs 8,00,000 with variable costs of Rs 5,60,000. Its fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000, of which Rs 1,80,000 would continue to be incurred even if the firm shut down, and shutting down would involve additional closure costs of Rs 20,000. The net advantage of continuing operations over shutting down is:
e: Continuing gives contribution Rs 8,00,000 - Rs 5,60,000 = Rs 2,40,000 minus fixed costs Rs 3,00,000 = loss Rs 60,000; shutting down loses unavoidable fixed costs Rs 1,80,000 plus closure costs Rs 20,000 = Rs 2,00,000; advantage of continuing = Rs 1,40,000.

q: Under the measured day work system of wage payment, a worker is paid:

options.A: A fixed day rate, set at a relatively high level, in return for maintaining a predetermined measured standard of work, the standard being fixed in advance
options.B: Strictly according to the number of units produced, with no guaranteed time wage
options.C: A bonus equal to the full wages of the time saved on each job
options.D: Time wages plus a share of the profits of the enterprise at the end of the year

e: Under measured day work the worker is paid a fixed, relatively high day rate in return for maintaining a predetermined measured standard of work fixed in advance.

q: Under a contract, the value of work certified is Rs 36,00,000 and the contract provides for retention money of 10 per cent of the value of work certified. The amount of retention money withheld by the contractee is:
e: Retention money = 10% of the value of work certified = 10% of Rs 36,00,000 = Rs 3,60,000.

q: The amounts deducted from a worker's wages on account of the worker's own share of provident fund and employees' state insurance contributions are, in cost accounts:

options.A: An additional labour cost borne by the employer over and above the gross wages
options.B: Part of the worker's gross wages themselves, and not an extra cost to the employer
options.C: Treated as factory overheads of the period
options.D: Excluded from the labour cost charged to jobs and charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account

e: The worker own provident fund and ESI contributions are deductions out of his gross wages, hence part of gross wages themselves and not an extra cost to the employer.

q: A joint cost of Rs 5,25,000 is to be apportioned between Joint Products A and B by the survey (points) method. On a technical survey, A (output 1,000 units) is assigned 3 points per unit and B (output 800 units) is assigned 2.5 points per unit. The share of the joint cost borne by Product A is:
Under the 100 per cent premium (bonus) plan of wage payment:

options.A: The worker receives a bonus of 50 per cent of the wages of the time saved
options.B: The worker receives no bonus at all, only time wages for the time taken
options.C: The bonus is shared between the worker and the foreman in a fixed proportion
options.D: The worker receives a bonus equal to the full wages of the time saved, so that his total earnings equal the wages for the standard (allowed) time

e: Under the 100% premium plan the bonus equals the full wages of time saved, so total earnings equal the wages for the standard time allowed for the job.

q: A machine was purchased for Rs 9,60,000. Its scrap value is estimated at Rs 60,000 and its effective working life at 15,000 hours. For computing the machine hour rate, the depreciation charge per machine hour is:

options.C: Rs 60
options.D: Rs 50

e: Depreciation per machine hour = (Rs 9,60,000 - Rs 60,000) / 15,000 hours = Rs 9,00,000 / 15,000 = Rs 60.

q: Cost audit is distinguished from financial audit mainly in that cost audit:

options.A: Verifies that the financial statements show a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the enterprise
options.B: Is concerned with verifying the correctness of the cost accounts and cost statements and the efficiency of the costing system, in the interest of management and, where prescribed, the Government
options.C: Is carried out only for banking and insurance companies
options.D: Dispenses with the examination of vouchers and supporting documents

e: Cost audit verifies the correctness of cost accounts and statements and the efficiency of the costing system, in the interest of management and, where prescribed, the Government.

q: A process is required to yield 9,500 units of good output. Normal wastage in the process is 5 per cent of the input. The quantity of input that must be introduced into the process is:

options.C: 10,500 units
options.D: 9,025 units

e: Good output is 95% of input after 5% normal wastage, so input = 9,500 / 0.95 = 10,000 units.

q: The cost accountant (management accountant) in an enterprise performs essentially a staff function, which means that he:

options.A: Has direct line authority over the production and sales managers and can issue orders to them
options.B: Is personally responsible for achieving the production targets of the factory
options.C: Collects, analyses and presents information and advises line management, while the authority to decide and to act remains with the line managers
options.D: Works independently of the line departments and need not consult them in preparing reports

e: The cost or management accountant performs a staff function: he collects, analyses and presents information and advises, while decision and action authority rests with line managers.

q: The rent of a factory building is Rs 6,00,000 for a period and is apportioned among the departments on the basis of the floor area occupied. The areas occupied are: Production Department X — 7,500 sq. ft.; Production Department Y — 4,500 sq. ft.; Service Department Z — 3,000 sq. ft. The share of rent apportioned to Production Department X is:
Wages paid to outworkers — workers who execute work at their own homes or premises, generally with their own tools, and are paid on a piece basis — are treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: Direct wages of the jobs executed by them, where the jobs can be identified
options.B: Selling and distribution overheads of the period
options.C: A charge to the Costing Profit and Loss Account, since no supervision is possible
options.D: Part of the cost of materials supplied to them

e: Wages of outworkers are direct wages of the jobs they execute where those jobs can be identified, since payment is on a piece basis for specific work.

q: Material of Rs 6,40,000 was issued from the stores to Job A. Out of this, material of Rs 40,000 was returned to the stores as surplus and material of Rs 25,000 was transferred directly to Job B. The net cost of material to be charged to Job A is:
e: Net material charged to Job A = Rs 6,40,000 - Rs 40,000 returned to stores - Rs 25,000 transferred to Job B = Rs 5,75,000.

q: In a Just-in-Time system, a 'kanban' is:

options.A: A buffer stock of material maintained to guard against supply interruptions
options.B: A monthly production programme prepared by the planning department
options.C: A card or signal that authorises the preceding work centre to produce, or the movement of, a specified quantity of material, so that production is pulled by actual demand
options.D: A report comparing the actual cost of production with the standard cost

e: In Just-in-Time, a kanban is a card or signal authorising the preceding work centre to produce, or the movement of, a specified quantity, so production is pulled by actual demand.

q: A department absorbs factory overheads at a rate per unit of output. Its budgeted factory overheads are Rs 4,80,000 for a budgeted output of 40,000 units. The overheads absorbed by a job comprising 2,500 units will be:
e: Absorption rate per unit = Rs 4,80,000 / 40,000 units = Rs 12; overheads absorbed by the job = 2,500 units x Rs 12 = Rs 30,000.

q: Expenditure on research which is of a general nature and cannot be identified with any particular product is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A factory overhead, spread over the products of the factory
options.B: A direct expense of the product nearest in design to the subject of the research
options.C: A deduction from the sales revenue of the period
options.D: Part of the cost of the closing stock of finished goods only

e: General research that cannot be identified with a particular product is treated as a factory overhead and spread over the products of the factory.

q: Under a periodic review system of inventory control, the stock of an item is reviewed at fixed intervals and an order is placed to bring the stock up to a predetermined target (maximum) level. The target level is 5,000 units, the stock in hand at the review is 1,800 units and 600 units are already on order. The quantity to be ordered is:

options.C: 5,000 units
options.D: 2,000 units

e: Quantity to order = target level - (stock in hand + stock on order) = 5,000 - (1,800 + 600) = 2,600 units.

q: In the primary distribution of factory overheads, the cost of power consumed by the departments is most appropriately apportioned on the basis of:

options.A: The floor area occupied by each department
options.B: The number of employees in each department
options.C: The number of light points in each department
options.D: The horse power of the machines and equipment installed in each department (with reference to the hours worked)

e: Power cost varies with the horse power of machines and equipment installed and the hours worked, so that is the most appropriate basis for apportioning power among departments.

q: The normal capacity of a factory is 50,000 units a year and its total fixed factory overheads are Rs 5,00,000. Actual production during the year is 38,000 units. The cost of idle capacity for the year, to be charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account, is:
e: Unabsorbed fixed overhead for idle capacity = (50,000 - 38,000) / 50,000 x Rs 5,00,000 = Rs 1,20,000, charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: The experience curve, as distinct from the learning curve, expresses the relationship between cumulative production and:

options.A: The total cost per unit, covering all elements of cost, which falls by a characteristic percentage each time the cumulative output doubles
options.B: The direct labour time per unit only, which falls as workers gain experience
options.C: The fixed cost per unit, which falls as output rises within the existing capacity
options.D: The selling price per unit, which falls as the market for the product matures

e: The experience curve relates cumulative production to total cost per unit (all cost elements), which falls by a characteristic percentage each time cumulative output doubles; the learning curve concerns labour time only.

q: The works cost (prime cost plus factory overheads) of a factory for a period is Rs 9,60,000. The opening work-in-progress is Rs 80,000 and the closing work-in-progress is Rs 1,04,000. The output of finished goods during the period is 39,000 units. The cost of production per unit is:
e: Cost of production = Rs 9,60,000 + opening WIP Rs 80,000 - closing WIP Rs 1,04,000 = Rs 9,36,000; per unit = Rs 9,36,000 / 39,000 = Rs 24.00.

q: A basic drawback of a cost-plus contract, from the point of view of the contractee, is that:

options.A: The contractor is forced to bear the whole risk of a rise in the prices of materials and labour
options.B: The final price of the work is known with certainty before the work begins
options.C: The contract price cannot exceed the estimate made at the time of tendering
options.D: The contractor has no incentive to economise, since his profit is a percentage of the cost incurred and rises with the cost

e: In a cost-plus contract profit is a percentage of cost incurred, so the contractor has no incentive to economise, since higher cost means higher profit - the main drawback for the contractee.

q: A product sells at Rs 200 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 120 per unit and fixed costs of Rs 2,40,000. It is proposed to reduce the selling price to Rs 180 per unit and to spend an additional Rs 60,000 on advertising, which will be a fixed cost. The variable cost per unit will remain unchanged. The break-even point under the proposal will be:

options.C: 5,000 units
options.D: 3,000 units

e: New contribution = Rs 180 - Rs 120 = Rs 60 per unit; new fixed costs = Rs 2,40,000 + Rs 60,000 = Rs 3,00,000; break-even = Rs 3,00,000 / Rs 60 = 5,000 units.

q: In the operating cost sheet of a transport undertaking, maintenance charges — such as repairs, overhauls and tyres and tubes — are classified as:

options.A: Standing charges, because they are incurred whether or not the vehicles run
options.B: A separate category of semi-variable charges, lying between standing charges and running charges, since they vary with running but not in direct proportion to it
options.C: Part of the capital cost of the vehicles, recovered through depreciation
options.D: Selling and distribution overheads of the undertaking

e: Maintenance charges vary with running but not in direct proportion to it, so in transport costing they form a separate semi-variable category between standing charges and running charges.

q: Under a contract, the value of work certified is Rs 20,00,000, which includes a gross profit of 25 per cent on the value of the work certified. The cost of work done but not yet certified is Rs 2,00,000. The total cost of the work done on the contract to date is:
e: Cost of certified work = Rs 20,00,000 x (100 - 25)% = Rs 15,00,000; total cost of work done = Rs 15,00,000 + cost of uncertified work Rs 2,00,000 = Rs 17,00,000.

q: A predetermined overhead absorption rate is computed as:

options.A: The actual overheads of the period divided by the actual level of activity of the period
options.B: The actual overheads of the previous period divided by the budgeted level of activity
options.C: The budgeted overheads of the period divided by the actual level of activity of the previous period
options.D: The budgeted overheads for the period divided by the budgeted (normal) level of activity for the period, fixed in advance of the period

e: A predetermined absorption rate is fixed in advance as budgeted overheads for the period divided by the budgeted (normal) level of activity for the period.

q: The total wages, including bonus, paid for a job are Rs 2,76,000. In all 75,000 units were produced on the job, of which 6,000 units were found defective, were rejected and scrapped, and the balance were accepted as good units. The labour cost per good unit is:
e: Good units = 75,000 - 6,000 rejected = 69,000; labour cost per good unit = Rs 2,76,000 / 69,000 = Rs 4.00.

q: A production order (works order) in a factory is a document which:

options.A: Records the cost of material, labour and overheads collected on a completed job
options.B: Is issued by the production planning department, authorising the production department to commence a job and to collect its costs against the order number
options.C: Is sent to a supplier for the purchase of materials required for production
options.D: Certifies the quantity of finished goods transferred to the finished goods store

e: A production or works order is issued by the production planning department, authorising the production department to commence a job and collect its costs against the order number.

q: The financial break-even point of a project is the level of annual sales at which:

options.A: The total revenue just equals the total accounting cost, including depreciation
options.B: The net present value of the project is exactly zero, so that it just earns the required rate of return on the capital invested
options.C: The cash inflows of that year just equal the cash outflows of that year
options.D: The contribution of that year just equals the fixed costs of that year

e: The financial break-even point is the sales level at which the project net present value is exactly zero, i.e. it just earns the required rate of return on capital invested.

q: An asset with a book value of Rs 80,000 is sold at the end of a project's life for Rs 1,10,000. The gain on the sale is taxed at 30%. The after-tax salvage value to be taken as a cash inflow in the project's appraisal is:
e: Gain on sale = Rs 1,10,000 - Rs 80,000 = Rs 30,000, tax at 30% = Rs 9,000; after-tax salvage value = Rs 1,10,000 - Rs 9,000 = Rs 1,01,000.

q: The discounted payback period, although it recognises the time value of money, still suffers from the limitation that it:

options.A: Ignores all cash inflows arising after the discounted payback period, however large they may be
options.B: Is worked out from accounting profits instead of cash flows
options.C: Cannot be computed when the cash inflows are uneven
options.D: Ignores the initial outlay of the project

e: Even discounted payback ignores all cash inflows arising after the payback period, however large, so a project with major later inflows can be wrongly rejected.

q: A sum of Rs 13,92,300 is required at the end of 4 years. Equal amounts are to be deposited at the end of each year in a fund earning compound interest, the future value annuity factor for 4 years at the fund's rate being 4.641. The amount of each annual deposit is:
e: Each annual deposit = amount required / future value annuity factor = Rs 13,92,300 / 4.641 = Rs 3,00,000.

q: In a replacement study, the existing machine whose replacement is being considered and the new machine proposed in its place are commonly referred to, respectively, as:

options.C: The incumbent and the entrant
options.D: The defender and the challenger

e: In replacement studies the existing machine is called the defender and the new machine proposed in its place is called the challenger.

q: A replacement is expected to save running expenses of Rs 2,50,000 a year before tax. It will carry additional depreciation of Rs 50,000 a year and the tax rate is 30%. The incremental annual cash inflow after tax from the replacement is:
e: Taxable saving = Rs 2,50,000 - Rs 50,000 depreciation = Rs 2,00,000; tax at 30% = Rs 60,000; cash inflow = Rs 2,50,000 - Rs 60,000 = Rs 1,90,000 (equivalently net profit Rs 1,40,000 plus depreciation Rs 50,000).

q: The cash flows of a project are estimated in real terms, that is, at constant prices. One major input is, however, expected to become steadily dearer in relation to other goods, its price rising faster than the general level of prices. In the appraisal, this input should be:

options.A: Left at its present price, since all figures are in real terms
options.B: Adjusted upwards to allow for the expected rise in its price relative to prices in general
options.C: Adjusted upwards by the full expected rate of general inflation
options.D: Excluded from the cash flows altogether

e: In real-terms appraisal only relative price changes matter, so an input expected to rise faster than general prices must be adjusted upwards for that expected relative rise.

q: A plant costing Rs 8,00,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum on the written-down-value basis. Its book value at the end of the second year is:
e: Book value after year 1 = Rs 8,00,000 x 80% = Rs 6,40,000; after year 2 = Rs 6,40,000 x 80% = Rs 5,12,000 on the written-down-value basis at 20%.

q: In the economic appraisal of a transport project, the excess of what the users would have been willing to pay for the journeys made over the fare they actually pay is counted as a benefit of the project. This excess is known as:

options.C: Transfer payment
options.D: Shadow price

e: The excess of what users would have been willing to pay over the fare actually paid is consumer surplus, counted as a benefit in the economic appraisal of a transport project.

q: The present value of all the costs (capital and running) of a machine over its life of 4 years is Rs 9,51,000. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at the cost of capital is 3.170. The equivalent annual cost of the machine is:
e: Equivalent annual cost = present value of all costs / annuity factor = Rs 9,51,000 / 3.170 = Rs 3,00,000.

q: The fumes and noise of a proposed industrial project will impose a cost on the public living nearby, although the enterprise itself will pay nothing for them. This cost will figure in the appraisal of the project:

options.A: In neither the financial nor the economic appraisal
options.B: In the financial appraisal but not in the economic appraisal
options.C: In the economic appraisal but not in the financial appraisal, because the economic appraisal counts all costs and benefits falling on society
options.D: In both appraisals, at the amount of the fine expected to be levied

e: Fumes and noise imposed on the public are external costs borne by society, not by the enterprise, so they enter the economic appraisal but not the financial appraisal.

q: A loan of Rs 6,00,000 carries interest at 10% per annum. A payment of Rs 1,80,000 is made at the end of the first year. The balance of the loan outstanding immediately after this payment is:
e: Balance after one year = Rs 6,00,000 + interest 10% of Rs 6,00,000 (Rs 60,000) - payment Rs 1,80,000 = Rs 4,80,000.

q: The value additivity principle associated with the net present value method means that:

options.A: The net present values of all the assets of an enterprise must add up to its balance sheet total
options.B: A project's net present value rises every time a further asset is added to it
options.C: The profitability indices of independent projects can be added together
options.D: The net present values of independent projects can be added together to measure their combined effect on the wealth of the owners

e: Value additivity means the net present values of independent projects can be added together to measure their combined effect on the wealth of the owners.

q: A project plant costs Rs 10,40,000 and is expected to have a salvage value of Rs 80,000 at the end of its life of 8 years. The annual depreciation on the straight-line basis is:
e: Annual straight-line depreciation = (Rs 10,40,000 - Rs 80,000) / 8 years = Rs 9,60,000 / 8 = Rs 1,20,000.

q: An enterprise that insists on a short cut-off payback period for accepting projects, even at the cost of rejecting some projects with a positive net present value, is in effect using the payback test chiefly as:

options.A: A measure of the project's profitability
options.B: A substitute for the cost of capital
options.C: A safeguard against risk and strain on liquidity, since capital recovered early is exposed to uncertainty for a shorter time
options.D: A means of ranking projects by their total cash inflows

e: A short cut-off payback period is used chiefly as a safeguard against risk and liquidity strain, since capital recovered early is exposed to uncertainty for a shorter time, not as a profitability measure.

q: A project's net cash inflow in a year will be Rs 1,60,000 or Rs 2,40,000, each with a probability of 0.5. The standard deviation of the inflow is:
e: Expected inflow = Rs 2,00,000; each outcome deviates by Rs 40,000, so variance = 0.5 x (40,000 squared) + 0.5 x (40,000 squared) and standard deviation = Rs 40,000.

q: Two projects are each quite risky when viewed alone. Taken together in the enterprise's portfolio of projects, however, they may add only a modest amount of risk. This will be so when:

options.A: Their cash flows tend to move in opposite directions, so that a shortfall in one is partly offset by a surplus in the other
options.B: Both projects have the same payback period
options.C: Both projects are of the same size
options.D: Their cash flows tend to move closely together in the same direction

e: Portfolio risk is modest when project cash flows move in opposite directions, so a shortfall in one project is partly offset by a surplus in the other.

q: Project A has an expected net cash inflow of Rs 4,00,000 with a standard deviation of Rs 80,000. Project B has an expected net cash inflow of Rs 2,00,000 with a standard deviation of Rs 60,000. Judged by risk per rupee of expected inflow, that is, by the coefficient of variation:

options.A: Project A is the riskier, because its standard deviation is larger
options.C: Project A is riskier, its coefficient of variation being 0.30 against 0.20 for B
options.D: Project B is the riskier, its coefficient of variation being 0.30 against 0.20 for A, although its standard deviation is smaller

e: Coefficient of variation: A = Rs 80,000 / Rs 4,00,000 = 0.20, B = Rs 60,000 / Rs 2,00,000 = 0.30; B carries more risk per rupee of expected inflow and is the riskier project.

q: A project will be accepted only if it shows an Average Rate of Return of at least 18%, computed on the average investment of Rs 5,00,000. The average annual profit (after depreciation and tax) that the project must yield to just meet this test is:
e: Required average annual profit = 18% of average investment Rs 5,00,000 = Rs 90,000 to just meet the average rate of return test.

q: A machine can be bought for Rs 4,00,000; the present value of its expected salvage value is Rs 60,000. Alternatively, it can be taken on lease, the present value of the lease rentals being Rs 3,65,000. On financial grounds:

options.A: Buying is preferable, the present value of its net cost (Rs 3,40,000) being lower than that of leasing by Rs 25,000
options.B: Leasing is preferable, being cheaper by Rs 25,000
options.C: Buying is preferable, being cheaper by Rs 35,000
options.D: Leasing is preferable, being cheaper by Rs 60,000

e: Net present cost of buying = Rs 4,00,000 - present value of salvage Rs 60,000 = Rs 3,40,000, which is Rs 25,000 lower than the lease cost of Rs 3,65,000, so buying is preferable.

q: Under the mid-year discounting convention sometimes used in project appraisal, the cash flows of each year are treated as if they arose:

options.A: At the beginning of the year, so that no discounting is needed for the first year
options.B: In one lump sum at the end of the project
options.C: Only in the middle year of the project's life
options.D: Evenly through the year, and are therefore discounted as if received at the middle of the year, which gives a higher present value than end-of-year discounting

e: Under mid-year discounting, cash flows are treated as arising evenly through the year and discounted as if received at the middle of the year, giving a higher present value than end-of-year discounting.

q: Stock is left out of the liquid assets used for the quick ratio chiefly because:

options.A: Stock is not an asset of the enterprise
options.B: Stock can be turned into cash only after being sold, and a sale on credit first creates a debtor, so that its conversion into cash is the slowest and least certain among the current assets
options.C: Stock is always valued at market price
options.D: Stock is a fixed asset in most enterprises

e: Stock is excluded from liquid assets because it converts to cash only through sale, and a credit sale first creates a debtor, making its conversion the slowest and least certain among current assets.

q: The gross capital employed of an enterprise, as distinct from its net capital employed, is:

options.B: The total of all assets, fixed and current, without deducting current liabilities; the net capital employed is this total minus the current liabilities
options.C: The long-term debt plus the current liabilities
options.D: The total assets minus the fixed assets

e: Gross capital employed is the total of all assets, fixed and current, without deducting current liabilities; net capital employed is that total minus current liabilities.

q: An enterprise may be solvent and yet illiquid. This position arises when:

options.A: Its current assets exceed its current liabilities by a wide margin
options.B: It has no long-term debt at all
options.C: The value of its total assets comfortably exceeds its total outside liabilities, but too much of its wealth is locked up in fixed or slow-moving assets, leaving it short of ready cash to meet dues as they fall due
options.D: Its proprietors' funds are negative

e: An enterprise is solvent but illiquid when total assets comfortably exceed outside liabilities yet too much wealth is locked in fixed or slow-moving assets, leaving it short of ready cash for dues.

q: The gross profit ratio of an enterprise has changed from one year to the next although neither its selling prices nor the cost per unit of any of its products has changed. A sufficient explanation of the change is that:

options.C: Its income tax rate has changed
options.D: The sales mix has shifted between its products, which carry different gross margins, so that the overall margin on the changed mixture of sales is different

e: With prices and unit costs unchanged, a shift in sales mix between products carrying different gross margins changes the overall gross profit ratio on the new mixture of sales.

q: In the interest coverage ratio, the profit figure used is the profit before interest and tax, rather than the profit after interest, mainly because:

options.A: Interest is not an expense of the enterprise
options.B: It is out of this profit, before the lenders are paid, that the interest has to be met, so the ratio shows how many times the interest charge is covered by the earnings available for paying it
options.C: The tax authorities prescribe this figure for the ratio
options.D: Profit after interest is never available to the analyst

e: Interest must be paid out of profit before interest and tax, so using PBIT shows how many times the interest charge is covered by the earnings available for paying it.

q: For computing the debtors turnover ratio and the average collection period, the term trade debtors is taken to include, besides the book debts for goods sold on credit:

options.C: Bills receivable arising from credit sales, since they represent amounts still to be collected from customers
options.D: Cash sales of the period

e: Trade debtors for turnover purposes include bills receivable arising from credit sales, since they are amounts still to be collected from customers, besides book debts.

q: Over a year, the gross profit ratio of an enterprise has risen appreciably while its inventory turnover ratio has fallen appreciably, with no change in prices or in the volume of business. This combination is a recognised warning sign of:

options.B: Overvaluation of the closing stock, which lifts the reported gross profit while the swollen stock figure depresses the turnover ratio
options.C: A fall in the cost of goods sold through better buying
options.D: An increase in cash sales at the expense of credit sales

e: Overvaluing closing stock inflates reported gross profit (lower cost of goods sold) while the swollen stock figure depresses the inventory turnover ratio - a recognised warning combination.

q: In a period of steadily rising prices, an enterprise that values its closing stock on the first-in, first-out (FIFO) basis, as compared with one using a weighted average cost, will generally report:

options.A: A lower closing stock and a lower gross profit
options.B: The same closing stock and the same gross profit
options.C: A lower closing stock but a higher gross profit
options.D: A higher closing stock, valued nearer to current prices, and consequently a higher gross profit and a stronger-looking current ratio

e: Under FIFO in rising prices, closing stock is valued at the latest, higher prices, so it is higher and gross profit (and the current ratio) look stronger than under weighted average cost.

q: The traditional standard of 2 : 1 for the current ratio is best regarded as:

options.A: A rough rule of thumb only, since the adequacy of a current ratio depends on the nature and turnover of the current assets, the operating cycle and the terms of credit available to the enterprise
options.B: A legal requirement for all companies
options.C: A test that every sound enterprise must pass in every year
options.D: Applicable only to banking companies

e: The 2:1 current ratio standard is only a rule of thumb; adequacy depends on the nature and turnover of current assets, the operating cycle and credit terms available.

q: At the end of a year, the trade debtors of an enterprise stand at Rs 3,40,000. During the year its net credit sales were Rs 12,60,000 and the cash collected from debtors was Rs 11,70,000. Its trade debtors at the beginning of the year were:
e: Opening debtors = closing debtors - credit sales + cash collected = Rs 3,40,000 - Rs 12,60,000 + Rs 11,70,000 = Rs 2,50,000.

q: An enterprise habitually settles its suppliers' bills, on average, 60 days after purchase, and the amount it owes its suppliers at any time averages Rs 2,40,000. Reckoning a year of 360 days, its credit purchases for the year work out to:
e: Creditors turnover = 360 / 60 = 6 times; credit purchases = average creditors x turnover = Rs 2,40,000 x 6 = Rs 14,40,000.

q: For every rupee locked up in its net fixed assets, an enterprise generates Rs 3 of net sales during the year. If its net sales for the year are Rs 54,00,000, the net fixed assets it employs are:
e: Fixed assets turnover = net sales / net fixed assets = 3, so net fixed assets = Rs 54,00,000 / 3 = Rs 18,00,000.

q: An enterprise prices its goods so as to earn a margin of 25% on the selling price. The goods it sold during the year had cost it Rs 11,25,000. Its net sales for the year were:
e: Margin is 25% on selling price, so cost is 75% of sales; sales = Rs 11,25,000 / 0.75 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: The owners of an enterprise claim 60% of everything it owns, the balance of the assets being financed by outsiders. If the total assets stand at Rs 45,00,000, the proprietors' funds amount to:
e: Proprietors funds = 60% of total assets = 60% of Rs 45,00,000 = Rs 27,00,000.

q: Under a loan covenant, an enterprise must maintain earnings before interest and tax of at least 4.5 times its interest charge. If the interest payable for the year is Rs 2,40,000, the minimum profit before interest and tax it must earn to satisfy the covenant is:
e: Minimum profit before interest and tax = covenant multiple x interest = 4.5 x Rs 2,40,000 = Rs 10,80,000.

q: An analyst values a company's share at 15 times its earnings. The Earnings Per Share of the company are Rs 24. On this basis, the value he places on the share is:

options.C: Rs 300
options.D: Rs 360

e: Value per share = price-earnings multiple x earnings per share = 15 x Rs 24 = Rs 360.

q: A company's policy is to keep the profit available for equity shareholders at 4 times the equity dividend it declares. If it wishes to declare an equity dividend of Rs 1,40,000, the profit available for equity shareholders must be at least:
e: Profit available for equity shareholders must be 4 times the dividend, so it must be at least 4 x Rs 1,40,000 = Rs 5,60,000.

q: A company distributes one-fourth of its earnings per share as dividend, and the dividend declared works out to Rs 7.50 per share. Its Earnings Per Share are:
e: Dividend per share is one-fourth of earnings per share, so EPS = Rs 7.50 x 4 = Rs 30.00.

q: A bank appraising a working-capital proposal finds that the enterprise's liquid assets of Rs 9,00,000 stand at one and a half times its current liabilities. The current liabilities are:
e: Liquid assets = 1.5 x current liabilities, so current liabilities = Rs 9,00,000 / 1.5 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: An enterprise has current assets of Rs 12,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs 5,00,000. It repays Rs 3,00,000 of a long-term loan in cash. Its current ratio after the repayment will be:
e: Repayment in cash reduces current assets to Rs 12,00,000 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 9,00,000 while current liabilities stay Rs 5,00,000 (a long-term loan is repaid), so current ratio = Rs 9,00,000 / Rs 5,00,000 = 1.8 : 1.

q: The book value per share of a company tends to rise over the years, even when it issues no fresh capital, mainly because:

options.A: Profits retained in the business add to the equity shareholders' funds while the number of shares remains the same
options.B: The market price of the share rises over the years
options.C: Depreciation charged each year increases the net assets
options.D: Its borrowings increase year by year

e: Profits retained in the business increase equity shareholders funds while the number of shares stays the same, so book value per share tends to rise even without fresh capital.

q: Of the common liquidity ratios, the cash ratio is regarded as the most stringent test of immediate liquidity because:

options.A: It is expressed in days rather than as a proportion
options.B: It counts in the numerator only cash, bank balances and near-cash equivalents, the assets that can be used at once to pay dues, against the current liabilities
options.C: It includes stock at its full selling price
options.D: It is the only ratio prescribed by law

e: The cash ratio counts only cash, bank balances and near-cash equivalents in the numerator against current liabilities, the assets usable at once to pay dues, making it the most stringent liquidity test.

q: Earnings Per Share figures of two companies are not directly comparable as a measure of their relative performance mainly because:

options.A: The two companies may have different accounting years
options.B: Earnings Per Share is worked out after tax
options.C: The figure depends on the number of shares into which each company's capital is divided, so a company with fewer, larger shares may show a high Earnings Per Share without being the more profitable in total
options.D: Market prices of the two shares are different

e: EPS depends on the number of shares into which capital is divided, so a company with fewer, larger shares can show a higher EPS without being more profitable in total, making direct comparison misleading.

q: A company keeps its Dividend Per Share unchanged, but the market price of its share rises sharply. Its dividend yield will:

options.A: Rise in the same proportion as the price
options.B: Remain unchanged, because the dividend is unchanged
options.C: Become equal to its earnings yield
options.D: Fall, because the same dividend is now being related to a higher market price

e: Dividend yield = dividend per share / market price per share; with dividend unchanged and price higher, the same dividend related to a higher price gives a lower yield.
